title: The Council Divides
story:
When Jarasandha sat down and Sunitha had given his voice to the warning, the kings of the earth looked at one another across the golden hall of Kundina. Into that silence rose Dantavakra, the king of Karusha.

He did not quarrel with the warning. What the king of Magadha and Sunitha have said for our well-being, he said, appears to me proper. I cannot blame these nectarine words out of malice, pride, or any desire for victory of my own. Who else could speak, in the midst of kings, words grave as an ocean and sanctioned by the science of polity?

What wonder is it that Vasudeva has come here? He has come for this maiden, as we have all come. We all unitedly laid siege to Gomanta; why do we find fault with that battle? Because of Kamsa's foolishness, those two heroes first lived in Vrindavana. To slay them, Kamsa invited Rama and Keshava and set an infuriated elephant against them. They slew the elephant and entered the arena, and by their own prowess slew Kamsa, king of Mathura, with his followers. What offence did they commit thereby, that we all, elderly in age, came to Mathura at another's instigation?

The hall stirred uneasily, for Dantavakra was describing their own war back to them. Terrified at our huge and overwhelming army, he went on, Rama and Keshava left their own city and their soldiers and fled to Gomanta. We pursued them there, and though we are expert in the art of fighting, we were defeated in the battle-field by those two boys. We laid siege to the hill, as Kshatriyas should, and set fire to it. Had they given up their lives quietly in that conflagration, taking it for a forest fire, we would have considered them humbled. We blame Janarddana because he fought against us. As matters now stand, wherever we go, we shall pick up a quarrel. Let us therefore contract friendship with Krishna.

Krishna has not come to this city of Kundina to pick a quarrel. He has come for the maiden; why should he fight with another? He is not an ordinary human being: the foremost of men in the land of mortals, the foremost of gods in the land of celestials, the Deity and the Creator of the worlds. In God there is no malice, pride or crookedness. The gods do not grow stupified or lean and are not visited by calamity, and they remove the calamities of those who bow unto them. Vishnu, the king of gods, has come here with Garuda to show his true form. And know this: Krishna never goes with his army to slay his enemies. That he has come accompanied by the leading Bhojas, Vrishnis, Andhakas and Yadavas indicates his desire of contracting friendship with you. Let us go, O kings, and offer the high-souled Keshava hospitality with arghya and water to rinse his mouth. If we make peace with Keshava, we shall be able to live freed from anxiety and fear.

Then Salwa, the foremost of speakers, rose, and the temper of the hall changed. What is the use of this fear? If we had trembled at the thought of Krishna and judged it proper to make peace with him, we would have left our weapons at that time. Why speak ill of our own army and extol another? That is not the duty of Kshatriya kings. We are all born in great royal families and have glorified our respective races; why should our sense be poor, like that of a coward?

He did not deny the warning. He embraced it and drew a different conclusion from it. I know Devaki's son Krishna as the immortal, eternal Prime Deity Vishnu, invincible unto the kings, powerful, adored of all the worlds, Vaikuntha, the preceptor of the entire world. I know all the objects of Vishnu: he has in view the destruction of king Kamsa, the relieving of the earth of her burden, our destruction, and the protection of the worlds. A great battle will take place between Vishnu and all the kings. I know truly that, consumed by the fire of his discus, we will go to the abode of Yama. Yet no one meets with untimely death, and no one survives when the proper time comes and the lease of his life runs out. Therefore a man should not entertain fear. When the ascetic virtue of the Daityas is annihilated, the divine Vishnu, conversant with yoga, brings about their destruction in due time. He sent down the mighty Bali to the nether region. He has performed many other feats like this; do not question the subject of fighting.

The debate broke against that rock and scattered. And through it all, Bhishmaka, king of Kundina, host of the council and father of the maiden and of the arrogant young Rukmi, had listened in silence. He had heard the warning of Jarasandha, the plea of Dantavakra, the defiance of Salwa, and weighed each against the one thing he could not bear to lose. Rising from his seat among the gathered princes, Bhishmaka resolved to go himself to Krishna, to propitiate, before any war began, the suitor the whole earth had gathered to deny. The council still rang with argument behind him as he stepped out into the evening, and Kundina, unknowing, went on lighting its lamps.
reflection: Every king in the hall seems to know who Krishna is; what divides them is what to do with the knowledge. Dantavakra reads the same facts as a summons to peace, Salwa as a summons to courage, and Bhishmaka, who alone among them is not deciding for an army but for his own children, reads them as a reason to bend. The council's war of words ends not with a king convinced but with a father moved.
next_story_tease: But the kings were not done debating, and soon Shalya would propose summoning the Yavana king Kalayavana.
hero_scene: In the golden assembly hall of Kundina, Bhishmaka rises silently from his seat among the arguing kings, Dantavakra pleading for peace on one side and Salwa answering with scorn on the other, and turns toward the door, resolved to go and propitiate Krishna himself.
